newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Bossi under attack for criticising Pope.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Bossi under attack for criticising Pope.

text.p: Umberto Bossi, the firebrand leader of Italy's separatist Northern League party, came under attack from all sides on Monday for accusing Pope John Paul of meddling in domestic politics.

Bossi, who regularly stirs controversy in the excitable world of Italian politics, turned his fire on the Vatican at the weekend, saying the Roman Catholic church had taken a step backwards under the leadership of Polish-born John Paul.

The comments drew unusually harsh condemnation from the Vatican paper, L'Osservatore Romano, and appeared to severely damage attempts at forging a political alliance between the League and the main centre-right opposition bloc.
"(Bossi) is a dwarf who thinks he is a giant," L'Osservatore said in an editorial, adding that the Northern League leader should respect the Pope, calling him "a true giant of contemporary history".
Opposition and government parties, in a rare display of public unity, also said Bossi had gone too far.
"Bossi's words are the fruit of a personal neurosis. He needs a psychiatrist," said Rocco Buttiglione, head of the Union of Christian Democrats, a centre-right opposition party.
The Northern League had been negotiating with the opposition to present a single candidate at the forthcoming mayoral election in the northern city of Venice.
But centrist parties in the opposition Freedom Alliance, which attract heavy support from Catholic voters, said the League should be ostracised.

"Bossi has attacked the only thing which has really kept this country united," said Clemente Mastella, the chairman of the CCD party. "If someone from the Freedom Alliance seeks an accord with Bossi, then I'll quit it," he added.
A spokesman for the Popular Party, which is part of the centre-left governing coalition, said all parliamentary parties should mobilise against Bossi.
"It makes sense to...join our energies for the benefit of the majority of northern Italians, of the right and of the left, who are tired of Bossi's delirium," Dario Franceschini said.
Bossi clashed with the church last year when he proclaimed independence for the northern "republic of Padania". His latest remarks were made at his holiday home in northern Italy.

"We're a long way from the times of Pope John XXIII, the great Lombard, who said the Church's interest in politics was finished and it was time for people to busy themselves only with their consciences," he told reporters.
John XXIII, who reigned from 1958 to 1963, was a native of Bergamo in the northern Lombardy region where the league has found some of its strongest support.
"Since then, the Polish Pope has arrived, has taken the Church and invested it much more with secular powers than with spiritual powers...Under him, the Church has taken a step backwards."

The Northern League has built its support on frustration with high taxes, central government bureaucracy and the slow pace of reform in Italy. It won 3.7 million votes in last year's general election.
Faced with criticism from all sides, Bossi late on Sunday tried to shift the target of his attacks.
"I don't think I so strongly attacked the Pope, maybe the Church. I just told the truth and, in this world of fickle people, the truth is a scandal."
